sectionTitle: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.3

specStatements.text: Waves can be reflected at the boundary between two different materials.
Waves can be absorbed or transmitted at the boundary between two different materials.
Students should be able to construct ray diagrams to illustrate the reflection of a wave at a surface.
Students should be able to describe the effects of reflection, transmission and absorption of waves at material interfaces.
Required practical activity 9 (physics only): investigate the reflection of light by different types of surface and the refraction of light by different substances.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 4 and 8.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

concepts.definition: The surface where one material ends and a different material begins, such as air and glass, air and water, or air and a brick wall. When a wave reaches a boundary it can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.
When a wave meets the boundary between two different materials and is sent back into the material it came from. Reflection happens to all waves, not only to light, and not only at mirrors.

A construction line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray meets it. It is drawn as a dashed line and is the line from which the angles of incidence and reflection are always measured.

concepts.term: Angle of incidence and angle of reflection
concepts.definition: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal. Neither is measured from the surface.
For a wave reflected at a surface, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. The incident ray and the reflected ray lie on opposite sides of the normal.

A diagram showing the surface, the incident ray with an arrow towards the point of incidence, the dashed normal at 90° to the surface at that point, and the reflected ray with an arrow away from it, drawn so that the marked angle of reflection equals the marked angle of incidence.

When a wave crosses the boundary and carries on travelling through the second material. The wave travels at a different speed in the new material, so unless it meets the boundary along the normal it also changes direction.

When a wave is taken in by the material at the boundary and does not continue as a wave. The energy carried by the wave is transferred to the energy stores of the absorbing material, usually its thermal store, so the material warms up.

The change of direction of a transmitted wave at a boundary, caused by the change in the speed of the wave. Light entering glass or perspex from air slows down and bends towards the normal; on leaving into air it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

At a real boundary all three effects usually happen together in different proportions. A window reflects a faint image, transmits most of the light and absorbs a little; a black matt surface absorbs most of the light and warms up; a hard wall reflects sound to give an echo, while curtains and carpet absorb sound so echoes die away.

concepts.term: Reflection by different types of surface
concepts.definition: In the required practical, a smooth shiny surface such as a plane mirror sends a narrow ray back as one clear reflected ray, while a rough surface such as white paper or crumpled foil scatters the light in many directions. Each individual ray still obeys the law of reflection; on a rough surface the normals point in many different directions.

Place the surface on a sheet of paper and draw round it. Shine a narrow ray from a ray box with a single slit at the surface. Mark the incident ray and the reflected ray with two dots each, well apart. Remove the surface, join the dots, draw the normal at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence, and measure the angles of incidence and reflection with a protractor. Repeat for different types of surface.

Place a transparent block on paper and draw round it. Shine a narrow ray into one face at a chosen angle of incidence and mark the ray going in and the ray coming out. Remove the block, join the marks to show the path inside, draw the normal at the point where the ray entered, and measure the angle of refraction. Repeat with blocks of different substances using the same angle of incidence each time, and compare how much each one bends the ray.

concepts.term: AT 4 and AT 8 in this practical
concepts.definition: Both of these apparatus and techniques statements are about observing how waves interact with matter. They are met here by using a ray box or lamp with a single narrow slit, transparent blocks and different surfaces to observe how light is reflected and refracted, and by using a protractor and sharp pencil to record the angles accurately.

concepts.term: Working scientifically and maths skills in this practical
concepts.definition: The investigation gives opportunities to identify and control variables, such as keeping the angle of incidence the same when different substances are compared, to measure angles to the nearest degree, to repeat readings and identify anomalies, and to plot and interpret a graph of angle of refraction against angle of incidence.

misconceptions.question: In a ray diagram, where is the angle of incidence measured from?
misconceptions.correct: From the normal, the dashed line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence.
misconceptions.misconception: You measure the angle of incidence from the surface, because that is the line the ray hits.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The surface is the obvious line in the diagram and is already drawn, while the normal has to be added by the student, so it feels like an optional extra.
misconceptions.correction: The two angles add up to 90°, so a ray at 30° to the mirror has an angle of incidence of 60°. Always draw the dashed normal first and measure both angles from it.

misconceptions.question: Which waves can be reflected, and where?
misconceptions.correct: Any wave can be reflected at the boundary between two different materials.
misconceptions.misconception: Reflection is something that only happens to light, and only when it hits a mirror.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every example met before GCSE is a mirror, and the everyday word 'reflection' means the image you see in one.
misconceptions.correction: Sound reflects from a cliff to give an echo, ultrasound reflects inside the body, and light reflects from a still pond. What matters is a boundary between two different materials, not a mirror.

misconceptions.question: What happens to light that lands on a sheet of white paper?
misconceptions.correct: It is reflected, but scattered in many directions rather than as one clear ray.
misconceptions.misconception: A rough surface does not reflect light at all, which is why you cannot see your face in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students use 'reflection' to mean 'making an image', so a surface with no image in it seems not to be reflecting.
misconceptions.correction: You can only see the paper because light reflects off it into your eyes. The surface is rough, so the normals point in many directions and the reflected rays are scattered instead of staying together.

misconceptions.question: What happens to a wave that is absorbed at a boundary?
misconceptions.correct: The energy it carries is transferred to the energy stores of the material, usually the thermal store.
misconceptions.misconception: When a wave is absorbed its energy is used up and disappears.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The wave really does stop, and nothing can be seen or heard afterwards, so it looks as though the energy has gone.
misconceptions.correction: Energy is never destroyed. A black surface left in sunlight absorbs the light and becomes measurably warmer, which is where the energy has gone.

misconceptions.question: What happens to a wave that is transmitted into a new material?
misconceptions.correct: It carries on, but at a different speed, and it changes direction unless it entered along the normal.
misconceptions.misconception: Transmitted means the wave goes straight through completely unchanged.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A window looks perfectly clear, so it seems that the light must pass through without anything happening to it.
misconceptions.correction: A ray entering a glass block at an angle is visibly bent, which shows the speed of the wave has changed at the boundary. The clear view through a window is because the two bends, going in and coming out, cancel each other for parallel faces.

misconceptions.question: When a wave reaches a boundary, how many of reflection, transmission and absorption occur?
misconceptions.correct: Usually all three occur at once, in different proportions for different materials.
misconceptions.misconception: Only one thing can happen at a boundary: the wave is either reflected, or absorbed, or transmitted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three words are taught as three separate cases, and diagrams normally show only one ray, which suggests only one outcome is possible.
misconceptions.correction: At a window you can see the street through the glass and a faint reflection of yourself in it at the same time, while the glass itself warms slightly in the sun. All three are happening at that one boundary.

misconceptions.question: Why does a ray of light change direction when it enters a glass block?
misconceptions.correct: Because the light travels at a different speed in glass than it does in air.
misconceptions.misconception: The light bends round the edge or the corner of the block, the way water flows round an obstacle.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The bend is seen at the edge of the block, so the edge looks like the cause, and 'bending round things' is a familiar everyday idea.
misconceptions.correction: The direction changes at the flat face, wherever on that face the ray enters, and not at the corners. It is the change of wave speed at the boundary that changes the direction.

misconceptions.question: Which way does a ray bend when it leaves a glass block and travels back into the air?
misconceptions.correct: It speeds up and bends away from the normal.
misconceptions.misconception: Light always bends towards the normal whenever it crosses a boundary.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first example students meet is air into glass, where the ray bends towards the normal, and that single case gets remembered as a rule.
misconceptions.correction: The direction of the bend follows the change of speed. Slowing down, as in air into glass, bends the ray towards the normal; speeding up, as in glass into air, bends it away.

misconceptions.question: What happens to a ray aimed along the normal at the face of a glass block?
misconceptions.correct: It carries straight on with no change of direction, although its speed does change.
misconceptions.misconception: Light is always bent when it enters glass, so a ray along the normal must bend as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Refraction is remembered as 'light bends in glass' rather than as a change of direction that depends on the angle of incidence.
misconceptions.correction: At an angle of incidence of 0° there is no sideways difference across the beam, so there is nothing to turn it. The ray goes straight on, more slowly, and is still refracted in the sense that its speed has changed.

misconceptions.question: Does the law of reflection hold for a rough surface?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Every single ray obeys it; the surface roughness makes the normals point in different directions.
misconceptions.misconception: Rough surfaces break the law of reflection, so light comes off them at bigger angles than it went in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Scattered light looks disorderly, and a rule that produces order seems not to apply where the result is disordered.
misconceptions.correction: Zoom in on a rough surface and each tiny facet is flat and tilted differently. Each facet reflects its own ray at an angle equal to its own angle of incidence, and the many different normals send the rays in many directions.

misconceptions.question: Why do echoes get quieter when a bare room is carpeted and curtained?
misconceptions.correct: Soft materials absorb more of the sound, so less of it is reflected back into the room.
misconceptions.misconception: The echo is caused by absorption, and soft materials reflect sound better than hard walls do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Absorb' and 'reflect' are both used loosely in everyday speech about sound, and students know soft furnishings change the sound of a room without being sure which way round.
misconceptions.correction: An echo is reflected sound returning from a hard boundary. Soft, porous materials absorb sound energy instead of returning it, which is why a carpeted room sounds dead and a bare hall sounds echoey.

misconceptions.question: Where should the reflected ray be drawn in a ray diagram?
misconceptions.correct: On the opposite side of the normal from the incident ray, at an equal angle to it.
misconceptions.misconception: The reflected ray is drawn on the same side of the normal as the incident ray, since the two angles are equal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn 'the angles are equal' as the whole of the law, and equal angles can be drawn on either side of the normal without breaking that rule.
misconceptions.correction: The ray has to travel away from the surface on the far side of the normal, or it would be going back along its own path. Draw the incident ray, the normal, and then the reflected ray as its mirror image in the normal.

misconceptions.question: When different substances are compared in the refraction practical, what must be kept the same?
misconceptions.correct: The angle of incidence, so that any difference in bending is caused by the substance alone.
misconceptions.misconception: You should change the angle of incidence as well as the substance, so that you collect more results.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know more readings are usually better, and confuse collecting a wide range of data with controlling a variable.
misconceptions.correction: If two things change at once you cannot tell which caused the difference. Fix the angle of incidence for every substance; a range of angles can be investigated separately with one substance.

misconceptions.question: What sort of beam should the ray box produce for this practical?
misconceptions.correct: A single narrow ray, made with one thin slit, so its path can be located precisely.
misconceptions.misconception: The wider and brighter the beam, the better, because you can see it more easily.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Faint rays are genuinely hard to see in a bright lab, so students open the slit or use several slits to make the beam obvious.
misconceptions.correction: A wide beam has no single path, so the pencil line and the angle both become uncertain. Use one narrow slit and dim the room instead, and mark the ray with two dots as far apart as possible.

misconceptions.question: How do you find the path of the ray inside a glass block?
misconceptions.correct: Mark where it enters and where it leaves, remove the block, and join the two points.
misconceptions.misconception: You have to measure the ray inside the block, so you hold the protractor against the glass and read it off there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The refracted ray is visible inside the block, so it seems natural to measure it while the block is still in place.
misconceptions.correction: The block cannot be drawn on and the protractor cannot sit flat on it. Draw round the block first, mark the entry and exit points, take the block away, and join the marks to reveal the path inside.

mcqs.stem: A wave travelling through the air reaches the surface of a still pond. Which statement about reflection is correct?

options.text: No reflection happens here, because reflection needs a polished mirror surface.
options.rationale: Students who have only met reflection at mirrors treat the mirror, not the boundary, as the requirement.

options.text: Reflection happens only if the wave travels from the water into the air.
options.rationale: Students assume reflection has a preferred direction, usually the one shown in the diagram they were taught from.

options.text: Some of the wave is reflected at the boundary between the air and the water.
options.rationale: Waves can be reflected at the boundary between two different materials; air and water are two different materials.

options.text: Reflection happens only where the water surface is perfectly smooth.
options.rationale: Students equate reflection with forming a clear image, so a disturbed surface seems not to reflect.

mcqs.stem: A walker shouts towards a cliff face and hears an echo a moment later. What has happened to the sound wave?

options.text: It has been reflected at the boundary between the air and the rock.
options.rationale: An echo is sound reflected back into the air at the boundary with a different material.

options.text: It has been absorbed by the rock, which is why the sound returns later.
options.rationale: Students who mix up absorption and reflection use the delay as evidence that the rock took the sound in.

options.text: It has been transmitted through the rock and out of the other side.
options.rationale: Students who think transmission leaves a wave unchanged expect it to reappear intact.

options.text: It has been refracted as it entered the rock and then bent back out.
options.rationale: Students reach for refraction as the label for any change to a wave at a boundary.

mcqs.stem: A black matt surface is left in bright sunlight and becomes noticeably warm. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: Light is absorbed at the surface, so the energy carried by the wave is destroyed.
options.rationale: Students who think absorption uses energy up cannot then explain the temperature rise.

options.text: Light is absorbed at the surface and the energy is transferred to a thermal store.
options.rationale: Absorption transfers the energy carried by the wave to the energy stores of the material, so it warms up.

options.text: Light is transmitted through the surface and carries its energy out the far side.
options.rationale: Students apply transmission to an opaque surface because the light clearly does not come back.

options.text: Light is reflected from the surface, and reflected waves always warm a material.
options.rationale: Students know black surfaces heat up and attach that fact to whichever process they remember first.

mcqs.stem: A ray of light travels from air into a thick glass block. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is transmitted into the glass with its speed and its direction both unchanged.
options.rationale: A clear block looks as though it does nothing, so 'transmitted' is read as 'unaffected'.

options.text: It is absorbed at the boundary, so no light gets into the glass at all.
options.rationale: Students who think one process rules out the others pick absorption once a boundary is mentioned.

options.text: It is transmitted only if it meets the surface exactly along the normal.
options.rationale: Students confuse the condition for travelling straight on with the condition for getting in at all.

options.text: It is transmitted into the glass, travelling at a different speed from before.
options.rationale: A transmitted wave carries on through the second material, and its speed there is different.

mcqs.stem: In a ray diagram for reflection, the angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and which line?

options.text: The surface itself, at the point where the incident ray strikes the mirror.
options.rationale: The surface is already drawn and the normal is not, so students measure from the line in front of them.

options.text: The reflected ray, taking the whole angle between the two rays together.
options.rationale: Students who are unsure where the normal goes measure the one angle the two rays obviously make.

options.text: The edge of the mirror, measured from the nearest end of the surface.
options.rationale: Students look for a fixed feature of the apparatus to measure from rather than a construction line.

options.text: The normal, the line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence.
options.rationale: Both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are measured from the normal.

mcqs.stem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the mirror surface is 30°. What is the angle of reflection?

options.rationale: Students measure from the surface instead of the normal and copy the given angle straight across.
Students add the 30° to 90° instead of subtracting, or give the total angle between the two rays.
The angle of incidence measured from the normal is 90° − 30° = 60°, and the angle of reflection equals it.
Students halve the given angle, thinking the reflected ray splits the angle at the surface.

mcqs.stem: A student draws a ray diagram of light reflecting from a plane mirror. Which feature shows that the diagram is correct?

options.text: The two rays are on opposite sides of the normal, with their angles to it equal.
options.rationale: The law of reflection requires equal angles measured from the normal, with the rays on opposite sides of it.

options.text: The two rays are on the same side of the normal, with their angles to it equal.
options.rationale: Students who learn only 'the angles are equal' can satisfy that rule on either side of the normal.

options.text: The angles to the mirror surface are equal, so no normal needs to be drawn.
options.rationale: Measuring from the surface gives equal angles too, so the error is invisible to the student.

options.text: The reflected ray leaves at 90° to the mirror, whatever the incident ray does.
options.rationale: Students remember that 90° matters in the diagram and attach it to the wrong line.

mcqs.stem: Thick curtains and a carpet are put into a bare room, and echoes in the room become much quieter. Which statement explains this?

options.text: The soft materials reflect the sound much better than the bare hard walls did.
options.rationale: Students know soft furnishings change the sound of a room but reverse which process they increase.

options.text: The soft materials transmit all the sound straight out of the building.
options.rationale: Students who treat transmission as total pass-through use it to explain any loss of sound.

options.text: The soft materials absorb more of the sound, so less of it is reflected back.
options.rationale: Soft, porous materials absorb sound energy at the boundary instead of returning it into the room.

options.text: The soft materials slow the sound down so that it cannot get back again.
options.rationale: Students explain the missing echo by a change of speed rather than a transfer of energy.

mcqs.stem: Standing in a lit room at night you can see the street outside a window and a faint reflection of yourself in it. What does this show?

options.text: Only one of reflection, transmission or absorption can happen at a boundary.
options.rationale: Students taught the three effects as separate cases assume they are alternatives.

options.text: All of the light is transmitted, and the faint image comes from the air itself.
options.rationale: Students committed to clear glass transmitting everything must place the reflection elsewhere.

options.text: Reflection, transmission and absorption can all happen at the same boundary.
options.rationale: The glass returns some light, lets most through and takes in a little, all at the one interface.

options.text: Glass reflects light only at night and transmits light only in the daytime.
options.rationale: Students generalise from when each effect is noticeable rather than from what the glass does.

mcqs.stem: In the required practical a narrow ray of light is shone first at a plane mirror and then at a sheet of white paper. What is seen?

options.text: The mirror gives one clear reflected ray; the paper scatters light in many directions.
options.rationale: A smooth surface keeps the reflected rays together; a rough surface has normals pointing many ways.

options.text: The mirror gives one clear reflected ray; the paper reflects no light back at all.
options.rationale: Students equate reflection with an image, so paper with no image seems not to reflect.

options.text: Both give one clear reflected ray, but the paper reflects at a much larger angle.
options.rationale: Students who think roughness alters the angle expect a single ray sent off at the wrong angle.

options.text: Both scatter the light, because any surface breaks up a narrow ray of light.
options.rationale: Students who have only seen scattering assume no surface can keep a beam together.

mcqs.stem: In the refraction part of the practical, a narrow ray passes from air into a glass block at an angle to the normal. What happens as it enters?

options.text: It slows down and changes direction, bending away from the normal.
options.rationale: Students remember that the ray bends but not which way the change of speed turns it.

options.text: It slows down and changes direction, bending towards the normal.
options.rationale: Light travels more slowly in glass than in air, and slowing at the boundary bends the ray towards the normal.

options.text: It carries straight on without bending, whatever the angle of incidence.
options.rationale: Students who think the block only slows the light expect no change of direction.

options.text: It bends round the corner of the block rather than at the flat surface.
options.rationale: The bend is seen near the edge of the block, so the edge looks like the cause.

mcqs.stem: The same ray reaches the far face of the glass block and passes back out into the air. What happens as it leaves?

options.text: It speeds up but bends towards the normal, as light always does.
options.rationale: Students turn the air-into-glass case into a rule that applies at every boundary.

options.text: It speeds up and bends away from the normal as it enters the air.
options.rationale: The wave travels faster in air, and speeding up at the boundary bends the ray away from the normal.

options.text: It carries on along the same line it followed inside the block.
options.rationale: Students who think transmission changes nothing see no reason for a second bend.

options.text: It slows down and bends away from the normal as it enters the air.
options.rationale: Students get the direction of the bend right but reverse the change of speed that causes it.

mcqs.stem: Why does a ray of light change direction as it passes from air into a perspex block?

options.text: The light bends around the edge of the block as it passes the corner.
options.rationale: The bend is visible at the edge of the block, which students read as the cause.

options.text: The perspex absorbs some of the light, and absorbing it turns the beam.
options.rationale: Students use absorption as a general explanation for anything happening to a wave.

options.text: The perspex is a solid, so it pushes the ray sideways as it goes in.
options.rationale: Students explain the bend by a mechanical push from the material rather than by wave speed.

options.text: The light travels at a different speed in perspex than it does in air.
options.rationale: A change of wave speed at the boundary is the cause of the change of direction.

mcqs.stem: In the practical a ray is aimed along the normal at the flat face of a glass block. What is observed?

options.text: The ray carries straight on without bending, though its speed does change.
options.rationale: At an angle of incidence of 0° there is no change of direction, but the wave still travels more slowly in the glass.

options.text: The ray bends towards the normal, as it does at every angle of incidence.
options.rationale: Students who remember refraction as 'light bends in glass' apply it whatever the angle.

options.text: The ray carries straight on and keeps exactly the same speed in the glass.
options.rationale: Seeing no bend, students conclude that the boundary has had no effect on the wave.

options.text: The ray is reflected straight back out along the path that it came in on.
options.rationale: Students expect a head-on ray to bounce back rather than to be transmitted.

mcqs.stem: AT 4 and AT 8 concern observing how waves interact with matter. Which technique makes the angles measured in this practical most reliable?

options.text: Use the widest and brightest beam available so that each ray is easy to see.
options.rationale: Students prioritise seeing the ray over defining it, and a wide beam has no single path.

options.text: Use one narrow slit in the ray box and mark each ray with two dots set well apart.
options.rationale: A narrow ray has a definite path, and widely spaced dots make the pencil line and the angle accurate.

options.text: Measure the angle inside the block by holding the protractor against the glass.
options.rationale: The refracted ray is visible inside the block, so measuring it in place seems the direct approach.

options.text: Measure the angles from the surface with a ruler rather than with a protractor.
options.rationale: Students who do not draw the normal look for a way to record the angle without one.

mcqs.stem: A student investigates how much glass, perspex and water each bend a ray of light. Which variable must be controlled for the comparison to be valid?

options.text: The angle of incidence, changed for each substance so that more data is collected.
options.rationale: Students confuse collecting a wide range of readings with controlling a variable.

options.text: The width of the beam, made as wide as possible for each substance in turn.
options.rationale: Students who value a bright visible ray name beam width as the thing to fix.

options.text: The thickness of the block, changed so each ray travels a different distance.
options.rationale: Students name a feature of the apparatus but describe changing it, not holding it constant.

options.text: The angle of incidence, kept the same for each of the three substances tested.
options.rationale: Only if the angle of incidence is fixed can any difference in bending be attributed to the substance.
